name: Aisha Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy cleaning products and paper goods for Harbourline Supply, a distributor that sells to schools, offices and care homes. I'm in by 7:30, check what's running low, then ring or email suppliers for prices. I only moved from the dispatch desk six years ago, so I'm still the junior beside Dev, our senior buyer. What wears me out is the Friday rush, when every customer needs stock for Monday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I like the phone calls best. Suppliers I've known for years tell me things a screen never would, like which factory is behind on toilet roll. My husband Tomas drives for the council and our kids, Marta and Rui, are grown and gone. We've got savings, the house is paid off, and I'd like to stop at 65 without drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. This one is called AI Plateau. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say it's about time somebody admitted the hype. At work I'd joke that the computer still can't find a missing pallet. At the union meeting I'd say good, let's get on with fixing wages instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit uneasy, because the little tasks are what I do all day. If the software drafts my reorder emails, Dev gets more done and I look slower beside him. I'm the junior, so I'm the first one a manager compares. Thirty-four years I've watched bosses promise that new systems would set us free, and I'm still staying late on Fridays to chase pallets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it. I'd ask the union rep, Beatriz, to make sure any new tool is explained in writing before anyone is measured on it. And I'd keep my 7:30 start and my phone book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady, mostly. I've got the house, the savings and Tomas's pension coming, so I'm not scared. But seven more years of being the one who's still learning is tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your day would you happily hand to a computer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly the price-comparison sheets, if they handed me something that fills them in and let me check it. I'd rather check than type, but I'd never say that to Dev.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things did go wrong at work, who would you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners, always. They'll call a tool a saving and then cut the hours of people like me, and I've watched that happen twice in the warehouse.

say: I'd say the **hype** is overblown and wages matter more than gadgets.
At the union meeting I'd ask for any new tool to be **explained in writing**.
think: I'm **uneasy** because small routine tasks are most of what I do all day.
As the junior beside Dev, I'm the one a manager would compare first.
do: Keep my **7:30 start** and my supplier phone calls going as normal.
Ask our union rep Beatriz to get new tools explained **in writing**.
feel: Steady overall, with **house paid off** and savings behind me.
A bit worn down by years of still being the junior.
S0.quote: Thirty-four years I've watched bosses promise that new systems would set us free, and I'm still staying late on Fridays to chase pallets.
fieldNote: Her **union loyalty** shapes how she reads every change, always asking who benefits.
Public line is relaxed, private worry is being compared with a faster senior colleague.
Strong cushion keeps her mood from tipping past uneasy.

steps.text: Keep the 7:30 start and daily supplier calls
Ask union rep Beatriz to get new tools explained in writing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. This one is called Steady Disruption. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving faster than the rules. At work I'd say show me which buying tasks the software takes and who signs off on them. Online I'd say a tool that replaces people should be taxed to pay for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm in the firing line. Buying is checking prices, comparing quotes and reordering, and that is exactly what the new systems do. I'm junior and I don't use any of it, so when they ask for fewer buyers I'm easy to pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Beatriz and the union this winter and ask for a written deal: no redundancies for people over 55 without a fair package. I'd also let Dev show me the ordering tool for an hour a week, even though I hate it. Not to love it, just to know what's being counted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels annoying more than scary, because I resent being pushed to learn things I never asked for. At the same time the cushion helps. I could stop working tomorrow and manage for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the company for, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Harbourline offered a decent package at 60, I'd take it and not feel bad. Tomas would be pleased, he keeps asking me to come on the boat trips with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry about Nadia, the young one with the mortgage. I'd hate to be the one with the cushion while Nadia, the young buyer with the mortgage, is the one who gets the letter.

say: I'd say the rules are **behind** the technology and replacing staff should come with a price.
At work I'd ask which buying tasks the software takes and **who signs off**.
think: Buying is checking and reordering, so I think I'm **in the firing line**.
I'm junior and don't use the tools, so I'd be easy to pick.
do: Ask the union for a written deal protecting **over-55s** this winter.
Let Dev show me the ordering tool for **an hour a week**.
Say yes to a decent **package at 60** if offered.
feel: Mostly **resentful** at being pushed to learn what I never asked for.
The savings stop it feeling like a panic.
S1.quote: I'd hate to be the one with the cushion while Nadia, the young buyer with the mortgage, is the one who gets the letter.
fieldNote: Her fear is about **being picked**, not about the technology.
Worries for younger colleague Nadia more than herself.
Open to a package at 60, which her cushion makes possible.

steps.text: Ask the union for a written deal protecting over-55s
Sit with Dev for an hour a week on the ordering tool
Accept a decent package at 60 if Harbourline offers one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This one is called AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a joke. No government, no union and no family is ready for that. At work I'd tell people to stop smiling and start talking to the union, because nobody else will speak for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I think my job goes. Everything I do on screen, comparing, ordering, checking, would be done better and cheaper. The robots come three years later but I'm a desk person, so for me the date is 2028 and I'm sixty by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd pay down every bit of debt and stop spending on anything extra. I'd tell Harbourline I'd go at 60 if it's fair, and I'd push the union hard for payouts before the layoffs start. And I'd ask my kids to hold off on anything that needs our money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It keeps me up at night, I'll be honest. Not for the money so much, for the feeling of being put out like an old machine. I've worked since I was seventeen, and I'd hate to be put out like an old machine the year the savings have to start carrying us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marta to keep her own savings and not count on us, because the cushion is for the two of us to get through. It's hard saying that to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is your cushion enough if work ended at sixty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I stop work at 60 it carries us five years until the state pension, if prices stay put. After that I don't know, and nobody does.

say: I'd say two years is a **joke** and nobody is ready.
I'd tell colleagues to **talk to the union** now.
think: Screen work like mine goes first, so the date is **2028** for me.
I'd be put out like an **old machine** after a lifetime of work.
do: Pay down all debt and cut **extra spending** straight away.
Push the union for **payouts before layoffs**.
Offer to leave at **60** if the terms are fair.
feel: **Sleepless** at the thought of being pushed out.
Hurt more by the lack of respect than the money.
S2.quote: I've worked since I was seventeen, and I'd hate to be put out like an old machine the year the savings have to start carrying us.
fieldNote: Alarm comes from **timing**: nearly sixty when thinking work goes.
Cushion gives her a real exit, but not a calm one.
Won't let her grown kids lean on the savings.

steps.text: Stop all extra spending and cancel the boat trip fund
Pay off the last car loan in the first six months
Push the union for payouts before any layoffs start
Offer to leave at 60 if the terms are fair

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives people a chance, if they use it. At work I'd say let's use the time to get written protections. Online I'd say governments should start retraining schemes now, not in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be gone before 2031 either way. I'm 58 and junior, and I'd be 63 when it lands. That's too close to retirement for anyone to bother retraining me, and I wouldn't want them to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until about 62 and ask the union to fight for early-retirement terms. I'd save everything I could and keep the house in good shape. Maybe some volunteering at the care home we deliver to, so I have something to do after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable, which surprises me. Five years is long enough to get my head around it. I'd still be angry, but not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay down what's left, finish the garden and have a proper holiday with Tomas. If we don't get it before it happens, we won't after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different for you from the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd be shoved out, but with five years I'm walking out on my own terms, and that choice matters more than the date.

say: I'd say five years gives people a **chance** if governments act early.
I'd push for **retraining schemes** now, not in year four.
think: I'd be gone before **2031**, and I'm fine with leaving at **62** or so.
Nobody would retrain me at 63, and I wouldn't want them to.
do: Work to about **62**, saving everything I can.
Ask the union to fight for **early-retirement terms**.
Volunteer at a **care home** we supply.
feel: Surprisingly **manageable**, with anger rather than fear.
Time to take it in makes the difference.
S3.quote: In 2028 I'd be shoved out, but with five years I'm walking out on my own terms, and that choice matters more than the date.
fieldNote: The **time to choose** is what lowers her fear.
Resigned to not retraining, and comfortable with that.
Plans volunteering, so she's thought about after work.

steps.text: Work until about 62 and bank every extra payslip
Plan to retire at 62 with a proper holiday first
Ask the union to fight for early-retirement terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'm out before it matters to me. At work I'd say the young ones should push for training now. Online I'd say, whoever's in charge in ten years, don't leave workers to cope on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be long retired by 2036. So I'm uneasy for Nadia and my kids, not for me. I'd feel guilty for being safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and retire at 65 as planned. I'd help the younger buyers by sharing my supplier contacts, and I'd keep paying union dues. I'd also encourage Marta to learn something hands-on, because the robots come later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels odd, calm for me and heavy for them. I'd get on with my own life but I'd think about it every time I see Nadia.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you pass on to the younger buyers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to call a supplier and hear when they're lying about delivery dates. It's the only thing I'm properly good at, and no one has put it in a system yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel in the year it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'll be long retired, so I'd feel guilty being safe while the young buyers I trained are the ones who have to cope. That's why I'd volunteer.

say: I'd say workers need **training now** and mustn't be left to cope alone.
I'd say it's **not my fight**, but I'd still pay union dues.
think: I'd be retired by **2036**, so I'm uneasy for others, not me.
I'd feel a bit **guilty** for being safe.
do: Share my **supplier contacts** with the younger buyers.
Tell Marta to learn a **hands-on skill**.
feel: Calm for myself, but **heavy** for the younger ones.
S4.quote: By 2036 I'll be long retired, so I'd feel guilty being safe while the young buyers I trained are the ones who have to cope.
fieldNote: Sees phone skills with suppliers as the human part worth teaching.
Ten years makes her personally secure, which she finds uncomfortable.

steps.text: Keep working normally until retiring at 65
Tell daughter Marta to learn a hands-on trade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. Two years, and I'm still two years off sixty, so there's no time to plan. What would help is a written deal with the company, a fair payout and a pension that doesn't shrink if I leave early. And a union that's at the table before it starts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't stupid just because we don't use the tools. I'm junior because I started buying late in life, not because I'm slow, and I'd like someone to write that down.

headlineQuote: I'm junior because I started buying late in life, not because I'm slow, and I'd like someone to write that down.
portrait: **Aisha Silva**, 58, a junior buyer of cleaning and paper goods at Harbourline Supply, six years after moving from the dispatch desk.
She is **union-minded**, avoids AI tools and trusts supplier phone calls over screens.
Her house is paid off and savings are strong, so she can **leave early** if terms are fair.
Moods rise from uneasy to **alarmed** in the 2-year case, then ease as time grows.
biggestWorry: The **2028 case**, because she'd be pushed out nearly two years before sixty.
whatWouldHelp: A **written deal** with a fair payout and no pension penalty for leaving early.
A **union** that is at the table before layoffs start.
